Pre-contract documents for a home purchase: purchase agreement, pre-approval letter, and proof of funds
Due diligence documents: home inspection report, appraisal report, title search and insurance, and environmental reports
Loan documents: mortgage application, loan estimate, final loan disclosure, and mortgage note
Insurance and warranty documents: homeowners insurance policy and manufacturer warranty documents
Closing documents: closing disclosure, deed, title, bill of sale, and closing statement
Other documents needed: government-issued identification, proof of income (pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns), and recent bank statements
Before making an offer, obtain the pre-approval letter from the lender and gather proof of funds for the down payment and closing costs
After making an offer, sign the purchase agreement and provide earnest money, typically 1-2% of the purchase price
Due diligence documents (home inspection, appraisal, title search and insurance, environmental reports) are handled 1-2 weeks after contract signing
Loan application and processing (mortgage application, loan estimate, final loan disclosure) occur 2-4 weeks after contract signing
Homeowners insurance policy and warranty documents are arranged 2-4 weeks after contract signing
Closing preparations (closing disclosure, ID, proof of income, bank statements) happen 1-2 weeks before closing
At closing, the deed and bill of sale are signed, title is received, the closing statement is reviewed, and the loan is funded

Common home inspection issues include roofing/gutters, plumbing leaks and corroded pipes, faulty wiring, foundation cracks, HVAC and insulation problems, pest infestation, environmental concerns, and malfunctioning appliances
Using the inspection report, a buyer can request repairs, request credits at closing, renegotiate the price, or walk away from the contract
Tips for negotiating with the seller: prioritize critical issues, provide evidence from the report, be reasonable, get everything in writing, and consult a professional

To ensure the seller follows through on repairs, get the agreement in writing, specify the scope of work, set a deadline before closing, hold back funds in escrow, verify repairs at a final walk-through, request a lien release, and keep records

A third-party contractor reviewing repairs provides an independent evaluation, specialized expertise, verification of completeness, additional negotiating power, and documentation of the property's condition at sale
When selecting a third-party contractor, get referrals, check that they are licensed and insured, request a written report, and insist on a neutral party with no affiliation to the seller
Getting a second appraisal before closing is not common practice but not unheard of; an initial appraisal is usually valid for 30 to 60 days
A final appraisal before closing may be worth considering if the property changed significantly, the local market fluctuated, or there are concerns about the initial appraisal's accuracy
If getting a final appraisal, notify the lender, choose a different appraiser for independence, and carefully review and understand the report
